Hooper's Paradox

ParadoxesArithmeticInvariants
Game: Cut a rectangle into four pieces and see how they can look like they make a bigger one.
How to play: Change the rectangle's sides and the cut, then tick "Show the flaw".
Look for the math

Can cutting a shape up and moving the pieces change its area? Of course not — but a clever drawing can make it look as if it did.

Geometric money

Hooper's classic puzzle cuts a 3 by 10 rectangle (30 square units) into triangles and trapezoids that seem to reassemble into a 2 by 6 and a 4 by 5 rectangle — 32 square units. Hooper called the apparent profit "geometric money". The pieces keep their areas; what changes is a tiny gap or overlap hidden along the joins. Fibonacci ratios make the mismatch so slight that the eye accepts the false picture.

What the check found

The logic test computes the areas of the four pieces by the shoelace formula for every rectangle up to 20 by 20 and every cut: their total always equals the original area. It also checks Cassini's identity for Fibonacci numbers, the algebraic reason near-miss dissections like this exist.

Tick "Show the flaw" and work out where the missing area would have to go.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
